newsitem.title: UK: Has pre-poll budget saved British Conservatives?.
newsitem.headline: Has pre-poll budget saved British Conservatives?.

text.p: Did Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke rescue the flagging Conservatives from defeat with his last annual budget before the next general election?

The British debated this question on Wednesday, the day after Clarke gave them a small cut in their income tax and a larger one in the price of whisky -- but the jury was still out and reactions from the media and analysts were mixed.
"For the government, yesterday's budget was the last shot in its economic locker before the election," said the Daily Telegraph.
"Has he done enough to keep Labour out?" the Daily Express newspaper said in a headline, posing the key question.
The election must be held by May 22 and the opposition Labour Party are some 20 percentage points ahead in pre-budget opinion polls.
A snap NOP opinion poll later showed only 17 percent of people thought the budget would make them better off.
But bookmakers appeared to think the budget will help Prime Minister John Major hang on to power. They shaved the odds on a Major victory to 6/4 from 7/4.
Many Conservative legislators had believed that the measures in the budget -- watched by millions in Britain for how it affects their personal finances -- could determine whether they retained seats.
To the Labour Party, on the other hand, the Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) must have looked like the only remaining obstacle to a return to power after almost 18 years.
In the event, the budget was seen as cautious, failing to match the more lurid expectations of those MPs who had pictured Clarke showering largesse on taxpayers to bribe voters.

A very modest penny in the pound cut in income tax, lower duties on hard liquor and modest increases in health and education spending were balanced by higher petrol and insurance taxes and a campaign to root out tax avoidance and evasion.

Clarke justified his prudence as responding to the needs of a rapidly expanding low-inflation economy in which prices could start to rise sharply again if the government provided much more stimulus to spending.
"The way we win the election is by showing we can run a market economy much more competently than our opponents," he told a news conference on Wednesday.

Conservative MPs loyal to Clarke and Prime Minister John Major praised the budget as just what was needed to show voters that the government had Britain's long-term interests -- and not the party's short-term prospects -- at heart.
But some right-wingers opposed to closer European ties muttered that Clarke had missed a golden opportunity to throw caution to the wind and cut deeply into spending and taxes.
"Yesterday's cut in income tax has done nothing to restore the reputation of the Conservatives for economic competence," polling expert Peter Kellner wrote in London's Evening Standard.

Other commentators doubted Clarke had much room to manoeuvre if he wanted to retain the confidence of the financial markets, which forced the pound out of the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) months after the last election.

"The Tories still bear the scars of having been ignominiously bumped out of ERM in 1992. That made it then, and makes it now, all the more important to demonstrate economic competence," said Donald Macintyre in the Independent.

Perhaps the most vital unanswered question is whether, despite Clarke's prudence, he will be forced to raise interest rates again before the election to damp down inflation, after a quarter point rise last month.

A Reuter survey of 35 economists on Wednesday showed they on average expect bank base rates to have risen a point to seven percent by the end of 1997 -- a move that would hit millions of houseowners struggling to pay off mortgages.
